title: A friend is in a relationship you believe is abusive
lede: The cancelled plans, the checked phone, the money they no longer control, the way they watch their partner before answering. You have hinted. They defended them, and now you see them less.

blocks.text: The cancelled plans, the checked phone, the money they no longer control, the way they watch their partner before answering. You have hinted. They defended them, and now you see them less.

items: Leaving is the most dangerous period, statistically. Pushing someone to leave before they have a plan can increase the risk to them, not reduce it.
People leave abusive relationships an average of several times before it holds. Returning is part of the process, not a failure of your advice.
Criticising the abuser directly usually backfires: it forces a defence and confirms the abuser's narrative that friends are hostile and should be avoided.
Isolation is the mechanism. Staying in contact — even shallow, cheerful contact — is the single most useful thing you can provide.

items.detail: Do not make your support conditional on them leaving. That is exactly what the abuser predicted you would do.
"He read your messages and you looked frightened" lands where "he is abusive" cannot.

items.move: Ask, and then believe, and then stay
items.detail: "Are you okay? You can tell me anything and I will not tell you what to do."
A spare key, a bag kept at yours, a lift, a phone, money for a taxi, your address written down.

items.move: Help them prepare rather than push them to act
items.detail: Documents, money, a code word, a plan for the children, a packed bag elsewhere. Preparation is the actual work.

items.move: Learn the local specialist service and share the number
items.detail: They can advise safely and confidentially, including on risk. You are not the expert; they are.

items.say: "I am not going anywhere and I am not going to lecture you. Whatever happens, ring me at any hour and I will come."
"When you said you had to ask him about Saturday, you looked scared. That is what worries me."
"Keep a bag at mine with your documents in it. No questions, no pressure. It just sits there."
"If you ever text me the word 'kettle', I will call you and say there is an emergency at mine, and I will come and get you."

items: Ultimatums — "if you go back I am done." It removes their last outside support.
Confronting the abuser. It escalates risk for your friend, not for you.
Telling them what you would do. It reads as judgement and it is not informed by their risk.
Sharing what they told you with the wider friend group. It can reach the abuser.
Giving up because they defended them. That defence is a survival behaviour.
Keep a private dated note of what you observe and are told, in case it is ever needed for police or court.
If they leave, expect a hard few months and stay close. Practical help beats advice.
Look after yourself too. Supporting someone through this is heavy and you need your own outlet.
Never say "I told you so," in any form, ever, including with your face.

limit: If you believe there is immediate danger — strangulation, threats to kill, a weapon, threats to children, or escalation around pregnancy or separation — call emergency services. These are recognised markers of severe risk and they justify overriding their wish for privacy.
